response:
READING

**The problem in numbers**

Rated works capacity: 14.2 ML/day. Forecast peak-week demand 2031: 15.4 ML/day. Gap: 1.2 ML/day. Capital envelope: £11.2 M, funds one scheme, not both.

---

**Testing SKELWITH against the gap**

The scheme forecast is 1.4 ML/day of distribution-loss saving. The Kilvaddy outturn ratio is 1.1 ÷ 1.3 = 84.6 %. Applying that: 1.4 × 0.846 = **1.18 ML/day**. Against a 1.2 ML/day gap, SKELWITH is already 0.02 ML/day short on its adjusted best case before a single day of drift is counted.

Now apply the drift. The three tranches run from April 2027 to March 2030. Taking the most favourable reading — the full 1.18 ML/day achieved by March 2030 — and drift-back at 0.1 ML/day per year, by the July 2031 peak week (approximately 16 months after programme completion) the residual saving is roughly:

1.18 − (16/12 × 0.1) = 1.18 − 0.13 ≈ **1.05 ML/day**

Effective demand at the works in peak week 2031: 15.4 − 1.05 = **14.35 ML/day** against a rated 14.2. SKELWITH leaves a 0.15 ML/day shortfall at exactly the time and season it is needed most. Storage can absorb a peak-week deficit in the short term, but planning to run into storage every summer as a structural feature is not a supply solution; it is storage depletion.

Beyond 2031 the position worsens at 0.1 ML/day per year unless the December 2029 regulatory settlement authorises further mains maintenance spend — which is uncertain. SKELWITH is a solution that is both demonstrably under-sized for 2031 and structurally eroding.

---

**Testing HARBOTTLE against the gap**

Cullivoe provides 3.0 ML/day of licensed capacity against a 1.2 ML/day need. That is 2.5 times the shortfall and it does not drift. The residual risk is the hands-off flow condition.

The condition bites when burn flow falls below 12.1 ML/day: 41 days in 2022, 29 days in 2025, all June to September. During curtailment the works runs at its 14.2 ML/day rating against a 15.4 ML/day peak demand, drawing on storage at 1.2 ML/day. Storage of 62 ML ÷ 1.2 ML/day = **51.7 days** of cover. The historical maximum curtailment is 41 days, giving approximately 10 days of headroom.

Two qualifications:

1. The 41-day figure is probably not 41 consecutive days across the summer; curtailment days will be scattered, allowing partial storage recharge between episodes. If anything the 51-day calculation overstates the risk.

2. Climate trends could push curtailment beyond historical levels. This is real but, on the data available, storage demonstrably covers the worst observed year by a margin of more than 20 %.

The interim period before Cullivoe commissions (June 2029) is worth checking. Current peak-week output is 13.6 ML/day against a rated 14.2, leaving 0.6 ML/day of headroom. With 1,900 homes phased across five years, demand growth is roughly 0.36 ML/day per year on a straight-line reading, giving a demand at peak 2028 of about 14.32 ML/day — 0.12 ML/day over rating. That is a temporary and modest exceedance well within the 62 ML treated storage buffer (more than 500 days at that gap) and fully resolved once Cullivoe commissions in June 2029 ahead of the 2029 peak summer.

---

**Financial and strategic comparison**

| | SKELWITH | HARBOTTLE |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | £5.9 M | £8.4 M |
| Remaining envelope | £5.3 M | £2.8 M |
| Capacity delivered by 2031 | ~1.05 ML/day (drifting) | 3.0 ML/day (firm) |
| Gap covered at 2031 peak | No (−0.15 ML/day short) | Yes (+1.8 ML/day headroom) |
| Requires future investment to maintain | Yes, continuously | No |
| Dependence on Dec 2029 settlement | High | Low |

SKELWITH costs £2.5 M less and the savings arrive earlier, both genuine merits. But the cost advantage does not compensate for a scheme that, on its own adjusted numbers, fails to meet the stated 2031 requirement before drift is even considered, and which then erodes unless the next regulatory period funds maintenance of the saving. The earlier delivery is also partially offset by the fact that demand growth in 2027–2028 is still within headroom, so the urgency of early delivery is less acute than it first appears.

HARBOTTLE costs £2.5 M more and commissions two years later than SKELWITH begins. But it purchases 3.0 ML/day of rated, permanent capacity against a 1.2 ML/day gap. The drought-curtailment risk, while real, is covered by existing treated storage on any historically observed year. There is nothing in the numbers that makes the two courses equivalent; one closes the gap and one does not.

---

READING completed. Proceeding to recommendation.

CALL
  HARBOTTLE

GROUNDS
  SKELWITH, on the Kilvaddy underperformance ratio and sixteen months of drift-back, delivers approximately 1.05 ML/day by peak summer 2031 against a 1.2 ML/day need and then continues to erode, whereas HARBOTTLE provides 3.0 ML/day of rated, permanent capacity whose single operational risk — hands-off flow curtailment — is demonstrably covered by 51 days of treated storage against a historical maximum of 41 curtailment days.
